title: Non-disruptive DR Drills for Oracle Databases Using Pure Storage ActiveDR — Part 1 of 4
summary: Learn how Everpure ActiveDR can simplify DR drills without the need to take an outage on your production systems.
body_markdown:
Disaster recovery drills have a reputation problem. They eat weekends, run on brittle manual runbooks, and get skipped more often than any auditor would like to admit. When a DR test does happen, it usually means a full failover, a tense stretch of validation, and an equally tense failback — all while production sits at risk.


This is part one of a four-part series on using Everpure ActiveDR to protect, test, and fail over Oracle databases without ever taking production offline. Read the series in order, or jump to the part you need:


- Part 1: Configure Everpure ActiveDR and protect your database volumes (this post)
- [Part 2: Access the database volumes at the DR site and open the database](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-pure-storage-activedr-part-2-of-4/)
- [Part 3: Run non-disruptive DR drills with simple scripting](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-pure-storage-activedr-part-3-of-4/)
- [Part 4: Controlled and emergency failovers and failbacks](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/non-disruptive-dr-drills-for-oracle-databases-using-pure-storage-activedr-part-4-of-4/)


Everpure ActiveDR is a replication capability built into every Everpure FlashArray at no additional cost. That includes FlashArray//C for capacity-optimized workloads, FlashArray//X for performance-optimized workloads, and FlashArray//XL for large-scale, low-latency consolidation. Wherever your Oracle databases run today, ActiveDR runs with them.


The standout benefit for Oracle teams: you can test your DR process without failing over or taking a production outage to do it. That’s what the rest of this series covers in detail. First, here’s the architecture we’re building.


The production database, ORCL, is a two-node Oracle RAC cluster on ASM. Its shared storage runs on an Everpure FlashArray//X named FLASHARRAY1. The DR site has two servers running the same OS and Oracle version, connected to a lower-cost FlashArray//C named FLASHARRAY2.


The steps below use the Everpure FlashArray management console, with the equivalent CLI command for each step so you can script the process.


### Connect the production and DR arrays


Before anything can replicate, the two arrays need a connection. This assumes network connectivity is already in place between the sites, with each array’s replication ports reachable.


On RedDotC (the DR array), go to Protection > Array Connections and copy the connection key:


purearray list –connection-key


On FLASHARRAY1 (the production array), go to Protection > Array Connections and click + to add a new connection:


- Paste in the connection key and enter the DR array’s IP address.
- Select async replication and choose a transport (Ethernet for IP-based replication, or FC).


purearray connect –management-address ###.###.###.### \\


–type async-replication –replication-transport ip \\


–connection-key 1231-d23524f-2525-cccasets3r


The connection from the production array to RedDotC now shows as connected:


### Create the ActiveDR pods


Next, create the pods that will hold the Oracle volumes on each array. Unlike Everpure ActiveCluster, where a single pod stretches across two arrays, ActiveDR needs a distinct pod on each side.


On the production array (FLASHARRAY1), go to Storage > Pods and click + to create a pod for the Oracle volumes:


purepod create oracle-pod-fa1


From Storage > Pods, select the three-dots in the Volumes panel to Move In volumes. On the Volumes panel, filter and select the oracle-prd volumes to add to the new pod.


When existing volumes are moved into a pod, they will be removed from any existing protection groups they are in. This screen allows us to automatically move the selected volumes into the new pod, and into a new protection group that will apply to the pod. Select the default oracle-pod-fa1::pgroup-auto.


purevol move oracle-prd-data00 oracle-prd-data01 oracle-prd-data02 oracle-prd-fra00 oracle-prd-fra01 oracle-prd-redo00 oracle-prd-redo01 oracle-pod-fa1


This runs with the database online — no downtime required. Non-disruptive change is core to how Everpure FlashArray works, from software upgrades to full hardware refreshes, so whether it’s a software upgrade or a storage refresh, the Everpure architecture never forces a database migration or outage to be able to perform the work.


Repeat the same steps on the DR array, creating a pod named “oracle-pod-fa2”:


purepod create oracle-pod-fa2


Both pods are created in a promoted state by default, meaning their volumes are read/write. Since replication only flows in one direction, only one pod can stay promoted — demote Oracle-DR to make it read-only:


purepod demote oracle-pod-fa2


### Link the pods and replicate


With oracle-pod-fa2 demoted, create the replication link. On the production array, go to Storage > Pods > and select the pod then at Pod Replica Links click +:


purepod replica-link create –remote-pod oracle-pod-fa2 –remote flasharray2 oracle-pod-fa1


The link starts in a baselining state — the initial seed copy of the volume data from production to DR:


Track replication progress under Analysis > Replication. Everpure FlashArray preserves data reduction across the wire, so a 4TB database achieving 4:1 reduction only needs to transfer 1TB for the initial baseline:


Once baselining finishes, the database volumes are replicated to the DR array and protected against a failure at the production site:


Ongoing changes replicate in near-sync fashion. Track lag under Analysis > Replication > Replica Links — after the initial seed, expect lag around one second unless write volume spikes or there’s a network issue between sites:


### What’s next


The database volumes are now protected and replicating to the DR site. Part 2 shows how to build and open an Oracle database from these volumes at the DR site. Part 3 covers non-disruptive DR testing. Part 4 covers real failover and failback scenarios.
